Variants.Content: Moat Cailin sits on the northern edge of the Neck; though most of the ancient stronghold lies in ruin, a few remaining towers still command the causeway running through the bogs. On either side of the Neck lie quicksands, reeds, venomous insects, bad air, and hard-to-read waterways, where heavy horse and baggage trains bog down the moment they leave firm ground; thus a small garrison that knows the terrain can hold up a southern host many times its size. The strength of Moat Cailin comes not from stone walls alone, but from the narrowness of the causeway, the impossibility of deploying on the flanks, and the length of supply lines. Holding the towers is not the same as conquering the Neck, and ignoring crannogmen guides can turn victory into disappearance.

Northmen regard Moat Cailin as their southern gate. Its towers may be ruined, yet so long as the causeway remains narrow and the defenders still have arrows and grain, a southern host must march column by column down a road already sighted for the bow.

What southern commanders fear most is not the wall they can see, but the trackless wetlands on either side of the road. The heavier the armor and the more numerous the wagons, the more Moat Cailin resembles a slowly closing hand.

The crannogmen know that the causeway is not the Neck itself. They read the way by reeds, bird calls, and the color of the water, and know that even after outsiders take a tower, they can still be lost in the mist ten paces away.
